distillation_scope_note: Disease-specific medical input is limited to the disease name: Thyroid storm. Etiology, trigger, cardiac phenotype, infection overlap, medication interruption, iodine exposure, pregnancy, surgery, and organ-failure severity are represented only as axes, mechanism edges, risk/context factors, event hazards, treatment modifiers, or case evidence.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Marked thyroxine and triiodothyronine excess with suppressed pituitary TSH, usually on a background of uncontrolled hyperthyroidism and amplified by an acute trigger.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: T3 tissue action and catecholamine sensitization
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Intracellular thyroid hormone action increases beta-adrenergic receptor responsiveness, mitochondrial oxygen use, Na/K ATPase activity, and tissue thermogenesis.
Increased basal metabolic rate, heat production, oxygen consumption, diaphoresis, catabolism, and fever-like hyperthermia out of proportion to ordinary infection alone.
Excess thyroid hormone and stress signaling produce tachycardia, palpitations, tremor, diaphoresis, hypertension or pressure lability, tachypnea, agitation, and arrhythmia vulnerability.

High-output circulation, rapid atrial or sinus tachycardia, oxygen supply-demand mismatch, stress cardiomyopathy, pulmonary congestion, and low-output collapse in patients whose cardiac reserve is exceeded.
Adrenergic and metabolic stress create anxiety, agitation, delirium, psychosis, obtundation, seizure risk, coma, and poor airway protection.

Hypermetabolism, hepatic congestion, cholestasis, hypoperfusion, drug exposure, and stress produce nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain, jaundice, transaminitis, coagulopathy, and occasionally acute liver failure.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Catabolic, electrolyte, respiratory, and muscle stress
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Thyroid-hormone-driven catabolism and adrenergic shifts cause weight loss, proximal weakness, tachypnea, lactate production, hypokalemic periodic paralysis in susceptible contexts, and respiratory fatigue in severe disease.
Uncontrolled hyperthermia, tachyarrhythmia, heart failure, shock, hepatic dysfunction, CNS failure, respiratory failure, renal injury, and treatment intolerance accumulate into near-term death risk.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Thyroid storm requires a substrate of active thyrotoxicosis even when the acute trigger is external.
TSH receptor stimulation can drive sustained hormone synthesis in Graves physiology.
Stopping or missing antithyroid treatment can remove control of hormone synthesis.
Iodine exposure can amplify hormone synthesis in susceptible autonomous or autoimmune thyroid tissue.
Acute illness, trauma, surgery, parturition, infarction, or other stress increases adrenergic and metabolic demand.
Infection can precipitate storm and independently adds fever, shock, hepatic, renal, and respiratory stress.
Operative, traumatic, and postpartum stress can rapidly decompensate uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis.
High circulating free T4 is the main biochemical substrate.
Free T3 reflects biologically active thyroid hormone excess and peripheral conversion.
Total T3 may be markedly elevated in thyroid storm, though illness and binding changes can modify the value.
Pituitary TSH is suppressed by thyroid hormone excess.
Circulating hormone excess drives tissue receptor and metabolic effects.
T3 tissue action increases metabolic rate and heat production.
Thyroid hormone sensitizes cardiovascular and neurologic tissue to adrenergic signaling.
Increased chronotropy, inotropy, blood volume, oxygen demand, and arrhythmia susceptibility stress the heart.
Hypermetabolism and trigger physiology raise body temperature.
Heat dissipation and adrenergic output produce sweating.
Patients often report heat intolerance before or during storm.
Sustained hypermetabolism and catabolism produce weight loss before acute crisis.
Marked tachycardia is one of the most consistent storm features.
Fever, acidosis, heart failure, and adrenergic drive raise respiratory rate.
Adrenergic excess and high-output physiology may raise systolic pressure before reserve fails.
Pressure can be hypertensive, labile, or collapse with heart failure and shock.
Enhanced beta-adrenergic tone produces tremor.
Tachycardia and ectopy create palpitations.
Adrenergic and CNS excitation can present as agitation or anxiety.
Thyrotoxicosis increases atrial automaticity and atrial fibrillation risk.
Sinus tachycardia, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmia, and electrolyte shifts can destabilize rhythm.
High-output failure, tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy, stress cardiomyopathy, and pulmonary congestion are major storm pathways.
Severe thyrocardiac stress can cause reversible systolic dysfunction.
Ventricular stretch and heart failure increase natriuretic peptide levels.
Supply-demand mismatch, stress cardiomyopathy, or myocarditis-like injury can raise troponin.
A failing thyrotoxic heart can transition from high-output stress to low-output shock.
Agitation, delirium, obtundation, and coma are core severe storm findings.
Severe encephalopathy lowers GCS.
Hyperthermia, metabolic disturbance, and CNS excitation can precipitate seizures.
Thyroid hormone increases gastrointestinal motility.
GI hypermotility and systemic stress commonly produce nausea or vomiting.
Abdominal pain can occur through GI hyperactivity, hepatic congestion, or a precipitating abdominal illness.
Cholestasis, congestion, and hepatic injury can raise bilirubin.
Storm-associated hepatic dysfunction can be cholestatic with conjugated bilirubin elevation.
Hepatic stress, hypoperfusion, and muscle stress can increase AST.
Hepatocellular injury can increase ALT.
Severe hepatic dysfunction or critical illness can prolong INR.
Hepatic dysfunction can progress to acute liver failure in severe storm.
Thyrotoxic myopathy and hypokalemic paralysis can present with weakness.
T3 and adrenergic stimulation can shift potassium intracellularly in thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.
Hypermetabolism, muscle work, shock, and respiratory failure can raise lactate.
Tachypnea, heart failure, weakness, aspiration, and coma can require ventilatory support.
Shock and congestion can cause AKI and raise creatinine.
Low perfusion, congestion, and critical illness increase AKI hazard.
Respiratory failure lowers oxygen saturation when support is inadequate.
Extreme hyperthermia accelerates CNS, hepatic, cardiac, and coagulation stress.
Atrial or ventricular arrhythmias can destabilize perfusion and organ function.
Heart failure adds pulmonary, renal, hepatic, and shock complications.
Death occurs through multiorgan failure rather than a separate disease manifold.
Unstable tachyarrhythmia or ventricular arrhythmia can cause sudden death.
Cardiogenic shock is a high-risk storm complication.
Acute liver failure signals severe systemic decompensation.
Respiratory failure and airway loss are fatal pathways.
AKI adds electrolyte, volume, and critical-care risk.

Recent nonadherence, discontinuation, inability to take, or withdrawal of antithyroid therapy.
Acute stressor such as infection, surgery, trauma, parturition, myocardial injury, DKA, contrast, or another acute illness that can precipitate storm.
Infectious trigger burden, preserved separately from any infection disease manifold.
Recent iodinated contrast, amiodarone, iodine supplement, or other iodine exposure relevant to thyroid hormone release or iodine treatment timing.
Recent surgery, major trauma, delivery, or perioperative physiologic stress.
Serum TSH, typically suppressed in thyrotoxicosis and thyroid storm.
Serum free T4 concentration.
Serum free T3 concentration.
Serum total T3 concentration, affected by binding proteins and critical illness.
TSH receptor antibody level when Graves physiology is present; this is etiology context and not required for all thyroid storm.
Measured core or peripheral body temperature; fever may be absent in some decompensated or treated presentations.
Heart rate; thyroid storm often produces marked sinus tachycardia or tachyarrhythmia.
Respiratory rate increased by fever, acidosis, heart failure, agitation, or respiratory failure.
Systolic pressure, often high or widened early but can fall with shock or beta-blocker intolerance.
Perfusion pressure; low values indicate shock or treatment intolerance.
Observed lability between hypertensive adrenergic state and hypotensive decompensation.
Diaphoresis or hypersudoresis.
Heat intolerance reported before or during decompensation.
Hand tremor or generalized tremulousness.
Unintentional weight loss attributable to hypermetabolism.
Proximal weakness, thyrotoxic myopathy, or episodic weakness from thyrotoxic periodic paralysis.
Subjective palpitations.
Atrial fibrillation or atrial flutter with rapid ventricular response.
Left ventricular ejection fraction; may be reduced by thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy or stress cardiomyopathy.
NT-proBNP concentration reflecting cardiac stretch or heart failure.
Troponin I from supply-demand mismatch, myocarditis-like injury, or stress cardiomyopathy.
Clinically important tachyarrhythmia, ventricular arrhythmia, or arrest hazard.
Heart failure hazard from high-output failure, tachycardia-mediated cardiomyopathy, stress cardiomyopathy, valve stress, or pulmonary congestion in thyroid storm.
Cardiogenic shock or low-output circulatory collapse hazard.
Anxiety, agitation, delirium, obtundation, or coma.
Agitation or severe anxiety as an observable mental-status component.
Glasgow coma scale score.
Seizure hazard during severe hyperthermia, metabolic disturbance, or encephalopathy.
Diarrhea or increased stool frequency.
Nausea or vomiting.
Abdominal pain from thyroid storm GI involvement or precipitating abdominal disease.
Total bilirubin concentration.
Direct bilirubin concentration.
Serum AST.
Serum ALT.
INR as a coagulation and hepatic synthetic marker.
Hazard of acute liver failure from storm-associated hepatic injury, congestion, hypoperfusion, or treatment-limited liver injury.
Serum potassium; may be low with thyrotoxic periodic paralysis or high with renal failure/acidosis.
Serum lactate from shock, hypermetabolism, seizures, or respiratory failure.
Serum creatinine.
AKI hazard from shock, congestion, rhabdomyolysis, dehydration, or multiorgan failure.
Peripheral oxygen saturation.
Respiratory failure hazard from heart failure, respiratory muscle fatigue, aspiration, pulmonary edema, or coma.
Disease-specific lifespan hazard for thyroid storm, mediated by multiorgan failure, arrhythmia, shock, hepatic failure, respiratory failure, AKI, and CNS failure.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: T4 and T3 usually rise together but are modified by peripheral conversion and critical illness.
Hyperthermia and adrenergic tone commonly move together.
Sustained rapid rates can precipitate or worsen thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy and heart failure.
Atrial fibrillation with rapid response is a major clinically important arrhythmia state.
Very low EF reduces tolerance for beta-blockade, tachycardia, and vasodilatory stress.
Pulmonary congestion and shock can progress to respiratory failure.
Heart failure is a dominant death pathway in severe storm.
Unstable arrhythmia can cause sudden cardiac arrest.
Severe hypo- or hyperkalemia increases arrhythmia risk.
INR elevation during hepatic dysfunction is an acute liver failure warning sign.
Obtundation and agitation can impair airway protection or require deep sedation.
Shock and congestion drive renal hypoperfusion and AKI.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Low-output thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy can collapse with excessive beta-blockade.
Hypotension limits negative chronotropy and inotropy.
Marked tachycardia and atrial fibrillation raise immediate benefit when perfusion reserve is adequate.

side_effects.interpretation: Negative inotropy and chronotropy can reduce perfusion pressure.
Patients with low-output thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy may decompensate after beta-blockade.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls adrenergic and rate-driven injury while requiring explicit hemodynamic and systolic-function context.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe liver injury changes thionamide selection and may favor non-hepatotoxic bridging strategies.
Withdrawal or nonadherence identifies the missing causal control lane.

side_effects.interpretation: Thionamides, especially PTU, can worsen liver injury in susceptible patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Blocks new hormone synthesis; choice and route depend on liver status, pregnancy context, and enteral feasibility.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Iodine can feed new synthesis if synthesis has not been blocked in susceptible thyroid tissue.
Recent iodine exposure changes gland iodine dynamics and treatment interpretation.

side_effects.interpretation: Adds iodine exposure that can matter if synthesis blockade is inadequate.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rapidly reduces release of preformed thyroid hormone when sequenced after hormone synthesis blockade.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Conversion blockade is more consequential when T3 activity is high.
Steroids can be useful in shock but may complicate infection control.

side_effects.interpretation: Immunosuppression can complicate active infection if source control is incomplete.

treatments.context_specific_role: Reduces peripheral T4-to-T3 conversion and supports stress physiology while other hormone-control lanes take effect.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cholestyramine requires enteral delivery.
Bowel dysfunction limits resin delivery and tolerance.

treatments.context_specific_role: Adds a hormone-removal lane by reducing enterohepatic thyroid hormone recycling.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Higher temperature increases immediate heat-injury and organ-failure risk.
Volume status and heat-loss capacity affect cooling strategy.

side_effects.interpretation: Cooling discomfort can worsen agitation if sedation and monitoring are inadequate.

treatments.context_specific_role: Direct state push for dangerous hyperthermia while causal hormone and adrenergic lanes are controlled.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Active infection can keep fever, shock, hepatic, and respiratory stress high.
When no trigger is active, direct thyroid and organ support dominate.

treatments.context_specific_role: Treats the observed precipitant through its own mechanism so thyroid storm is not treated as isolated hormone excess.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Airway protection and ventilatory support directly reduce hypoxemic and aspiration death pathways.
Vasopressors, inotropes, invasive monitoring, and escalation decisions are central when shock is present.

sigma_modulation.clinical_rationale: ICU monitoring and rescue reduce uncontrolled physiologic volatility.

side_effects.interpretation: Mechanical ventilation and invasive lines can add infection risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Contains respiratory, hemodynamic, electrolyte, renal, and neurologic failure while thyroid-directed therapy reshapes the upstream field.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Extracorporeal removal becomes more consequential when thionamides are contraindicated or failing.
TPE lowers hormone burden but does not alone restore circulation in shock.

side_effects.interpretation: Extracorporeal therapy can cause hemodynamic instability.
Plasma exchange and replacement fluid can change coagulation markers.

treatments.context_specific_role: Rescue hormone-removal vector when conventional pharmacotherapy is failing, contraindicated, or too slow for severe organ failure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe potassium abnormality is an arrhythmia pathway that may need urgent correction.
CRRT may be better tolerated than intermittent dialysis during shock.

treatments.context_specific_role: Controls renal, acid-base, volume, and electrolyte death pathways while the storm field is being reshaped.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Mechanical support is most relevant when shock persists despite pharmacologic support.
Irreversible neurologic injury changes the benefit of invasive support.

side_effects.interpretation: Cannulation and anticoagulation add bleeding risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Bridge for reversible thyrocardiac collapse while hormone removal and organ support act.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Unstable storm physiology makes thyroidectomy hazardous without adequate support.
Radioiodine feasibility depends on iodine exposure and uptake.

side_effects.interpretation: Airway and anesthetic risk can rise during unstable thyroid surgery.

treatments.context_specific_role: Definitive control of the thyroid source after stabilization, or rescue source control when medical and extracorporeal measures cannot control the field.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises the substrate for thyroid storm but does not define a subtype.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Active hyperthyroidism is the background field.
More active thyroid hormone production increases free T4.
More active thyroid hormone production increases T3 burden.
The interruption itself is observed.
Hormone synthesis can rebound when control is stopped.
Infection adds pyrogenic heat to hypermetabolism.
Infection adds shock, hepatic, renal, and respiratory stress.
The stressor is observed.
Acute stress increases adrenergic tone.
Recent iodine exposure is directly observed.
Iodine can amplify or sustain hormone production in susceptible thyroid tissue.
Lower cardiac reserve magnifies the same hormone and rate burden.
Systolic dysfunction and ischemia lower shock threshold.
Cardiac failure is a major mortality pathway.
Older patients are more vulnerable to delirium and decompensation.
Frailty lowers reserve during heart failure, infection, and coma.
Reduced physiologic reserve worsens outcome.
Thyrotoxic periodic paralysis produces hypokalemia and weakness in susceptible patients.
Hypokalemic paralysis can dominate the presentation.
Severe hypokalemia increases arrhythmia risk.
Pregnancy and postpartum stress can precipitate decompensation in active hyperthyroidism.

present.trajectory_modulation: Does not prove thyroid storm but allows organ injury to accumulate.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Delay allows hyperthermia, tachyarrhythmia, and organ injury to progress.
Delayed multilane control worsens survival.

supportive_care: Preserve the thyroid hormone chronology: known hyperthyroidism, untreated disease, antithyroid drug interruption, iodine or amiodarone exposure, and timing of any infection, surgery, trauma, parturition, myocardial event, or DKA-like stressor.

Use presentation-time vitals, mental status, GI symptoms, heart rhythm, heart failure findings, thyroid function labs, potassium, liver tests, bilirubin, INR, creatinine, lactate, oxygenation, and echocardiography as ordinary evidence when available.

Store final paper diagnosis, Burch-Wartofsky or Japanese Thyroid Association score conclusions, Graves confirmation, thyroid ultrasound interpretation, radioactive uptake, and antibody-based etiology as confirmatory/context evidence when they are diagnostic conclusions rather than raw presentation findings.

Trend heart rate/rhythm, blood pressure, temperature, mental status, urine output, oxygenation, free T4/T3, TSH, electrolytes, liver tests, bilirubin, INR, creatinine, lactate, troponin, BNP, and bedside or formal echocardiography in moderate to severe disease.

Sequence thyroid-directed therapies explicitly when known: hormone synthesis blockade, hormone release blockade, peripheral conversion blockade, adrenergic control, enterohepatic binding, extracorporeal removal, organ support, and definitive thyroid source control.
Assess cardiac reserve before or during beta-adrenergic control; low ejection fraction, shock, or pulmonary edema should be represented as treatment context rather than ignored.

Treat infection, myocardial ischemia, sepsis, toxicologic syndromes, heat stroke, DKA, and abdominal emergencies through their own evidence paths without deleting overlapping fever, tachycardia, diarrhea, altered mental status, or shock evidence.

Escalate support context for coma, seizure, hypoxemia, pulmonary edema, cardiogenic shock, unstable arrhythmia, rapidly worsening liver failure, severe electrolyte abnormality, AKI, or refractory hormone excess.
